name: Northern Roglai
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Northern Roglai (nort2994) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Lee 1963 'Inches, feet, and yards in Northern Rơglai' (Anthropological Linguistics 5:14-16), is a false keyword hit ('feet' = measurement) — an ethnographic note per Glottolog, irrelevant, not fetched sources (JSTOR only). Beyond the sweep list I located and read six open sources, ( lists them): the Cobbey et al. 1977 Northern Roglai Vocabulary pronunciation pages (archive.org Rosetta scan; silent on stress, but treats the last syllable of polysyllables as distinguished), Lee 1998 on Cat Gia Roglai (ANU PL A-89; uses 'pretonic'/'tonic syllable' for Roglai disyllables, implying final stress), Norquest 2005 (ANU PL 569; states Chamic shifted main stress to the final syllable and that Northern Roglai keeps the Proto-Chamic prosodic structure unchanged — the best explicit statement read), Brunelle, Brown & Phạm 2022 Phonetica (PMC author manuscript; Raglai words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables with a final stressed main syllable and unstressed presyllable), Brunelle et al. 2025 Phonetica (silent), and Cobbey 1979 (silent). Reading: fixed word-final stress (Chamic sesquisyllabic type), but every statement read is comparative or definitional, not a first-hand stress rule. Highest-priority unread source: Lee 1966 'Structure of Northern Roglai as a representative Chamic language' (Indiana PhD, pp. 21-69; ProQuest only); also Cobbey & Cobbey 1980 SIL microfiche field notes, Tạ Văn Thông 2009 (Vietnamese, print), Thurgood 1999 (UH Press/JSTOR).org APIs and Europe PMC/PMC; Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Google Books and DuckDuckGo were rate-limited or blocked.

[...] [p.180, §3.3 Northern Cham] Tsat and Northern Roglai form the Northern Cham subgroup within the other major branch of Highlands Chamic. While N. In Anthony Grant & Paul Sidwell (eds), Chamic and Beyond: Studies in mainland Austronesian languages (Pacific Linguistics 569), 147-188. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. DOI 10.15144/PL-569.147

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (42 pp., text layer). Both quoted passages are there verbatim at the stated locators: (1) PDF page 13 = printed p.159, section 2 'From Proto-Malayo-Chamic to Proto-Chamic': 'This contact had the effect of shifting the main stress of the prosodic word from the penultimate syllable to the final syllable, which then became heavy and could include a moraic final consonant.' (2) PDF page 34 = printed p.180, section 3.3 'Northern Cham': 'Tsat and Northern Roglai form the Northern Cham subgroup within the other major branch of Highlands Chamic. While N. Roglai has continued the prosodic structure of PC relatively unchanged, Tsat has gone through a fundamental evolution.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Northern Roglai retains the Proto-Chamic (Mon-Khmer-induced) sesquisyllabic word shape: main stress is on the final (main) syllable of the word, which is heavy; any preceding syllable(s) are unstressed, reduced presyllables. Corroborated at family level by Brunelle, Brown & Phạm 2022 §1.2 ('sesquisyllables, words whose final stressed syllable, the main syllable, is preceded by a reduced unstressed syllable, the presyllable'), whose Northern Raglai wordlist was built from such sesquisyllables and monosyllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Northern Roglai; Norquest mentions secondary stress only for reconstructed PMC trisyllables (p.~163).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Northern Roglai. Norquest notes N. Roglai kept 'ear' (PC *tali:ŋa > N. Roglai) without the metathesis seen elsewhere (p.~178), a segmental not a stress exception.
new_statements.domain_note: Prosodic word (lexical items in citation form; comparative data drawn from Lee 1966 wordlists). The statement is indirect: it asserts that Northern Roglai preserves the PC prosodic structure, which the same paper defines as word-final main stress. No field description of Northern Roglai stress was opened; the primary sketch (Lee 1966) is inaccessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottocode nort2994 (ISO rog), the northern dialect group spoken in Khánh Hòa and northern Ninh Thuận (Brunelle et al. 2022 §1.2). Norquest 2005 labels the variety 'N. Roglai' / 'Northern Roglai' (data ultimately from Lee 1966); Brunelle, Brown & Phạm 2022 describe 'Northern Raglai' of Phước Đại commune, Bác Ái district, Ninh Thuận. Lee 1998 concerns Cat Gia Roglai (cacg1235) with Northern Roglai (NR) comparanda; Southern Roglai (sout3010) material in Brunelle 2022/2025 was not used for the statement.

new_statements.quote: This contact had the effect of shifting the main stress of the prosodic word from the penultimate syllable to the final syllable, which then became heavy and could include a moraic final consonant. [...] Tsat and Northern Roglai form the Northern Cham subgroup within the other major branch of Highlands Chamic. While N. Roglai has continued the prosodic structure of PC relatively unchanged, Tsat has gone through a fundamental evolution.
new_statements.citation: Norquest, Peter (2005). Word structure in Chamic: prosodic alignment versus segmental faithfulness. In Grant & Sidwell (eds), Chamic and Beyond (Pacific Linguistics 569), 147-188. DOI 10.15144/PL-569.147.
new_statements.locator: p. 159 (§2 'From Proto-Malayo-Chamic to Proto-Chamic') and pp. 180-181 (§3.3 'Northern Cham')
new_statements.reading: Northern Roglai keeps the Proto-Chamic word-prosody: main stress on the final (main) syllable, with any preceding syllable an unstressed presyllable — i.e. fixed word-final stress. This is a comparative, second-hand statement (Norquest's data come from Thurgood 1999, ultimately Lee 1966); it is corroborated by Lee 1998's consistent 'pretonic syllable / tonic syllable' terminology for Roglai disyllables (p. 32, 35) and by Brunelle et al. 2022 §1.2 ('sesquisyllables, words whose final stressed syllable, the main syllable, is preceded by a reduced unstressed syllable, the presyllable'). No first-hand descriptive stress rule for Northern Roglai was read: Lee 1966 (the only phonological sketch) is ProQuest-only.

sources.quote: In Austroasiatic and Chamic, this usually occurs in sesquisyllables, words whose final stressed syllable, the main syllable, is preceded by a reduced unstressed syllable, the presyllable (Butler 2014; Thomas 1992). ... It is unclear if there is register spreading in Raglai dialects [...] Monosyllabic words without codas were preferred; when they were not available, we tried to find sesquisyllables with open main syllables and monosyllables with sonorant codas
sources.note: §1.2: 'In Austroasiatic and Chamic, this usually occurs in sesquisyllables, words whose final stressed syllable, the main syllable, is preceded by a reduced unstressed syllable, the presyllable (Butler 2014; Thomas 1992).' §2.2: Northern Raglai wordlist built from monosyllables and 'sesquisyllables with open main syllables'. Family-level statement applied to Northern Raglai (Phước Đại, Bác Ái, Ninh Thuận); no NR-specific stress rule.

This iambic PC stress pattern...' — Proto-Chamic level; N. Roglai appears only as reflex data in tables.

sources.quote: 1) In polysyllabic words an r is not pronounced except in the last syllable. Between vowels the r is dropped and the adjoining vowels are pronounced as one long vowel. ... 2) In the last syllable of a polysyllabic word or in a monosyllabic word r is pronounced as a semivowel
sources.note: The scanned pronunciation guide (consonants, vowels, length, nasalization, dialectal r) says nothing about stress. It does note polysyllabic structure with a distinguished last syllable: 'In polysyllabic words an r is not pronounced except in the last syllable' — consistent with a final main syllable but not a stress statement. Silent on stress.
Consonant and vowel tables only; no information on stress, syllable structure or prosody; references = Ethnologue, Cobbey & Cobbey 1977, Lee 1966, Brunelle et al. 2022.
